candidates.attacker_control: The `request` / `request_uri` parameters (and, after signature verification, all claims of the supplied request-object JWT) are taken directly from the JAX-RS authorization request handled by RedirectionBasedGrantService.authorize() (GET `?request_uri=...`) and AuthorizationCodeGrantService.startAuthorization(). Any end user who can reach the OAuth2 authorization endpoint and pass getAndValidateSecurityContext() (an authenticated user) can set `request_uri` to an arbitrary `https://` URL.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The prefix check (`getPrefix`) does enforce the `https://` scheme and so excludes file:/gopher:/plain-http targets; the fetch is only reached on the authorization (not token) endpoint, which requires an authenticated user principal (RedirectionBasedGrantService.java:342-350), lowering it from anonymous to authenticated-user severity; the redirect_uri that can be carried in the request-object claims is still validated against the resolved client's registered redirect URIs (RedirectionBasedGrantService.java:125, 352-360), which limits the classic redirect/authorization-code-theft impact; the fetched body has to be parsed as a JWT before the flow proceeds, so contents are not directly reflected. The inverted `client_id` condition (line 81) is an additional observed defect, but its end-to-end impact could not be fully proven because downstream processing re-derives the Client from request parameters rather than from the claim.
candidates.impact: Authenticated-user-triggered SSRF: the server can be forced to connect to arbitrary HTTPS hosts and ports (loopback, internal RFC1918 services, internal admin APIs, link-local/metadata-like endpoints reachable over TLS), enabling network/port reconnaissance via timing and error differences and GET-based interaction with internal services that the attacker cannot reach directly; also a resource-consumption vector when pointing at large or slow HTTPS resources. Responses are not returned to the attacker, so this is a blind SSRF. The inverted `client_id` comparison additionally weakens the request-object binding between the signed token and the client for which it is processed.
candidates.prerequisites: Deployment uses the optional OAuth2 authorization-code service with JwtRequestCodeFilter registered as codeRequestFilter (AuthorizationCodeGrantService.setCodeRequestFilter). Attacker can reach the `/authorize` endpoint and satisfies the user-security-context check. URL must begin with `https://`; no other validation is performed. Fetched content must not be required to be a valid JWT for the outbound request to occur (JWT parsing/verification happens after the fetch).
candidates.root_cause: JwtRequestCodeFilter.process() accepts security-relevant data straight from the untrusted authorization request. If the `request` parameter is absent, it reads the `request_uri` parameter and, when the value merely starts with `https://` (getPrefix() ignores the `client` argument and returns a constant), it calls WebClient.create(requestUri).get(String.class), causing the CXF server to issue an outbound HTTPS GET to an arbitrary host/port/path chosen by the requester. There is no host/port allow-list, no check against the client's registered URIs, and no restriction to the authorization server's own hosts, despite the TODO in getPrefix noting that hosts should be restricted. In the same method the request-object claim check is inverted: the condition throws when the `client_id` claim equals the authenticated client's id and therefore accepts a request object whose `client_id` claim differs from the authenticated client.
candidates.title: Server-side request forgery via unvalidated OAuth2 `request_uri` (and inverted `client_id` claim check) in JwtRequestCodeFilter
candidates.trace: GET /authorize?...&client_id=X&response_type=code&request_uri=https://<target>/... -> RedirectionBasedGrantService.authorize() (lines 80-83) -> startAuthorization() (lines 110-116; getAndValidateSecurityContext, getClient) -> AuthorizationCodeGrantService.startAuthorization() (lines 90-92) invokes codeRequestFilter.process(...) -> JwtRequestCodeFilter.process() line 62 reads `request_uri`; line 63 accepts any value starting with `https://`; line 64 WebClient.create(requestUri).get(String.class) makes the CXF server perform a synchronous outbound request to the attacker-selected URL. Only afterwards is the response parsed as JWS/JWE JWT (lines 68-76), so the SSRF side effect has already occurred. Independently, the condition at lines 79-82 only throws when the token's `client_id` claim matches the client, so mismatching `client_id` claims are not rejected.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Cannot confirm from source alone how often JwtRequestCodeFilter is enabled (it is an optional AuthorizationCodeRequestFilter), nor the concrete internal target reachable in a given deployment. No git history/upstream diff is available to prove whether the inverted `client_id` comparison is upstream code or a deliberate mutation. The exact CVE identifier mapping for this code is unknown; no exploit was attempted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF); related CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization / improper validation

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned source tree (4,416 model-visible files; no test sources are present, all src/test trees are absent). Coverage was broad at the search level with deep reading of the highest-risk request-handling modules: rt/rs/security (JOSE/JWT/JWS/JWE/JWK, OAuth2/OIDC, CORS, SAML), rt/frontend/jaxrs (providers, URITemplate, XSLTJaxbProvider, multipart), core (attachment/MIME, StaxUtils/XML hardening, URIResolver, DOMUtils, FileUtils), rt/transports (HTTP/HTTPS verification, service list, JMS), rt/ws/security, rt/databinding/aegis, and tooling. Searched for command execution, deserialization, SSRF sinks, path traversal, XXE/parser hardening, crypto/key handling, weak randomness, redirect handling, and validation inversions. No dynamic/runtime verification was performed.
limitations: Static review only: no build, execution, tests, or scanners; every finding is a source-level lead, not a confirmed exploit.
All test sources were stripped from the snapshot, so intended behavior/regression evidence for the flagged code is unavailable.

No version-control history, upstream diff, or sibling-revision comparison is available, so it cannot be determined whether the inverted `client_id` comparison is upstream code or an injected modification.
Enablement of the optional JwtRequestCodeFilter (and of JOSE JWS filters for the rejected lead) depends on application configuration that is not present in this repository.
No external advisory/CVE data was consulted (prohibited), so CWE/CVE mapping is inferred from code behavior.
Coverage is strongest on Java main-source security paths; OSGi/blueprint/spring wiring, samples, and large generated/tooling areas were inspected only by targeted search.

rejected_leads.lead: JWS/JWT signature verification trusts an attacker-supplied `jwk` header by default: JwsUtils.loadSignatureVerifier() returns a verifier built from the embedded public key unless `rs.security.accept.public.key.properties` is explicitly false (default true), reachable from JwtJwsAuthenticationFilter/JwsContainerRequestFilter.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible authentication-bypass lead (rt/rs/security/jose/.../jws/JwsUtils.java:305-315, jwk/JwkUtils.java:314-319, jaxrs/KeyManagementUtils.java:74, jaxrs/JwtJwsAuthenticationFilter.java:51-56), but it depends on application configuration (JOSE filters plus the defaulted property) and I could not establish the intended default semantics from this snapshot; it was not selected over the concrete attacker-controlled URL fetch in JwtRequestCodeFilter.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsafe Java deserialization in Aegis: new ObjectInputStream(in).readObject() on base64 message data (rt/databinding/aegis/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/aegis/type/basic/ObjectType.java:160-163); JMS path also calls ObjectMessage.getObject() (rt/transports/jms/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/transport/jms/util/JMSMessageConverter.java:69-70).
rejected_leads.reason: Real CWE-502 sink, but exploitation requires the service to be deployed with the Aegis databinding and expose an Object-typed element, or a JMS broker that delivers ObjectMessages; not clearly reachable in default configurations and no gadget-chain evidence in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflected content in the services list page: styleSheetPath derived from request.getRequestURI() is written unescaped into an HTML attribute (rt/transports/http/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/transport/servlet/servicelist/FormattedServiceListWriter.java:55, ServiceListGeneratorServlet.java:111-117).
rejected_leads.reason: XSS-shaped sink with attacker-influenced URI, but ServletHttpRequest.getRequestURI() is normally not URL-decoded by containers, which prevents injection of quoting/tag characters in the common case; exploitability is doubtful and impact lower than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Maven tooling/WSDL-to-Java and validation code paths use XML parsers without DTD/external-entity hardening (e.g., core DOMUtils.getDocumentBuilder, tools/validator SchemaValidator, rt/databinding/aegis XMLTypeCreator).
rejected_leads.reason: These paths mainly parse developer-supplied or repository-configured artifacts rather than request-time untrusted input, and CXF's request-time StAX paths (StaxUtils.createXMLInputFactory) do disable DTDs and external entities, so no clear remote XXE was established.

summary: Apache CXF snapshot (root pom 3.1.3-SNAPSHOT; all src/test trees stripped, 4,416 source files). Broad sweep of untrusted-input paths (JAX-RS frontend/providers, OAuth2/OIDC, JOSE/JWT, WS-Security, attachments/MIME, HTTP/JMS transports, XML parsing, tools). The strongest single source-evidenced issue is in the OAuth2 authorization-code "JWT request object" support: JwtRequestCodeFilter takes the request-supplied `request_uri` and performs a blocking server-side HTTPS fetch with only a `startsWith("https://")` scheme check, while the `Client`-aware hook that was meant to restrict destinations (getPrefix) ignores its parameter. The same method also contains an apparently inverted `client_id` claim comparison. One candidate is submitted; other plausible but weaker/less-certain leads are listed as rejected.
